intro.generic: I'll keep you oriented. You do the thinking.
intro.b01: Let's give your folder a memory. One command — and you'll see everything change.
intro.b02: Git now exists. Next comes Git's most important rule: nothing gets saved without your say-so.
intro.b03: Good news: someone already made commits here. Your job is to read their story.
intro.b04: Time to work on two things at once. Branches make that possible.
intro.b05: Now build something real on your branch — main stays safe.
intro.b06: Time to bring the two lines together. Watch what happens to the labels.
intro.b07: A merge with a twist: Git needs your judgment on one spot.
intro.b08: Everyone makes mistakes. The skill is undoing them on purpose.
intro.b09: Sometimes work has to pause. Git has a shelf for that.
intro.b10: Last beginner mission: meet the remote — where collaboration lives.

effects.REPOSITORY_INITIALIZED: Git created the hidden `.git` folder. This folder is now a repository, ready for its first commit.
effects.FILE_STAGED: The current version of the file moved into the Staging Area.
effects.COMMIT_CREATED: A new commit was saved. The current branch label now points to it.
effects.BRANCH_CREATED: A new branch label appeared at this commit.
effects.BRANCH_DELETED: A branch label was removed. Its commits stay in history.
effects.BRANCH_MOVED: A branch label moved to a different commit.
effects.HEAD_MOVED: HEAD moved — you are now looking at a different commit.
effects.MERGE_FAST_FORWARD: No new commit: the branch label simply slid forward along existing history.
effects.MERGE_COMMIT_CREATED: A merge commit was created — it has two parents, one from each side.
effects.CONFLICT_CREATED: Git paused the merge: this file needs your decision.
effects.CONFLICT_RESOLVED: The conflict is resolved — you chose the final content.
effects.RESET_PERFORMED: The branch label moved backward. Local history was rewritten.
effects.STASH_CREATED: Your changes were lifted onto the stash shelf. The Working Tree is clean.
effects.STASH_APPLIED: The stashed changes came back onto the Working Tree.
effects.CHERRY_PICK_CREATED: The change was copied into a new commit on this branch.
effects.COMMITS_REPLAYED: Commits were replayed with new identities.
effects.TAG_CREATED: A tag now names this commit.
effects.REMOTE_UPDATED: Your knowledge of the remote was refreshed.
effects.WORKTREE_CHANGED: The Working Tree changed — Git sees the difference now.

concepts.repository: Repository — Git's memory attached to your folder
concepts.working-tree: Working Tree — your files right now
concepts.staging-area: Staging Area — versions selected for the next commit
concepts.snapshot: Snapshot — a saved copy of the whole project
concepts.commit: Commit — one saved snapshot with a message
concepts.hash: Hash — the unique ID of a commit
concepts.parent: Parent — the commit that came before
concepts.branch: Branch — a movable label pointing at a commit
concepts.head: HEAD — the marker for where you currently are
concepts.pointer: Pointer — a reference that can move
concepts.branch-tip: Branch tip — the newest commit a branch points to
concepts.divergence: Divergence — two branches holding different commits
concepts.merge: Merge — combining two lines of work
concepts.fast-forward: Fast-forward — merging by just moving a label
concepts.merge-commit: Merge commit — a commit with two parents
concepts.merge-base: Merge base — the last commit both sides share
concepts.conflict: Conflict — Git needs your decision on a change
concepts.ours: Ours — the version from your current branch
concepts.theirs: Theirs — the version from the incoming branch
concepts.reset: Reset — moving a branch label backward
concepts.revert: Revert — a new commit that undoes an old one
concepts.history-rewrite: History rewrite — changing commits that already exist
concepts.stash: Stash — a shelf for work in progress
concepts.temporary-work: Temporary work — changes you are not ready to commit
concepts.remote: Remote — another repository your Git talks to
concepts.origin: Origin — the conventional name of the main remote
concepts.remote-tracking: Remote tracking — your local notes about the remote
concepts.fetch: Fetch — updating your knowledge of the remote
concepts.pull: Pull — fetching and merging in one step
concepts.push: Push — publishing your commits to the remote
concepts.rebase: Rebase — replaying commits onto a new base
concepts.pick: Pick — keep a commit during replay
concepts.reword: Reword — change a commit message during replay
concepts.squash: Squash — combine a commit with the previous one
concepts.drop: Drop — remove a commit during replay
concepts.cherry-pick: Cherry-pick — copying one commit onto your branch
concepts.patch: Patch — the change a commit contains
concepts.new-identity: New identity — replayed commits get new hashes
concepts.stash-stack: Stash stack — multiple shelved entries, newest on top
concepts.context-switch: Context switch — pausing one task to work on another
concepts.reflog: Reflog — the diary of every ref movement
concepts.orphaned-commit: Orphaned commit — a commit no branch points to
concepts.detached-head: Detached HEAD — HEAD pointing at a commit, not a branch
concepts.branch-reference: Branch reference — the named pointer a branch provides
concepts.three-way-merge: Three-way merge — comparing both sides against the merge base
concepts.conflict-resolution: Conflict resolution — choosing the final content
concepts.binary-search: Binary search — halving the search space each step
concepts.regression: Regression — a bug introduced by a past commit
concepts.submodule: Submodule — a pointer to another repository
concepts.subtree: Subtree — another project merged into your history
concepts.blob: Blob — the object storing file content
concepts.tree: Tree — the object storing a folder structure
concepts.commit-object: Commit object — a snapshot with author, message and parents
concepts.ref: Ref — a human-friendly name for a commit
concepts.content-addressing: Content addressing — IDs are hashes of the content

option.0: It copies your files to a safe backup location.
option.1: It creates the hidden `.git` folder where Git stores history.
option.2: It deletes your folder and starts a new empty one.

init-means.explain: `.git` is Git's memory. Your files stay exactly where they are.

commit-without-add.prompt: You change `app.ts` and run `git commit` without `git add` first. What happens?

option.0: Nothing is committed — Git only commits what you staged.
option.1: Git automatically stages and commits everything for you.
option.2: The commit works, but it skips the Working Tree.

commit-without-add.explain: Commits contain only what's in the Staging Area. That's the safety mechanism: you always choose what gets saved.

newest-commit.prompt: `git log` lists commits. Which commit is at the TOP of the list?

option.0: The newest commit — history is printed newest first.
option.1: The oldest commit — history starts from the beginning.
option.2: A random commit — Git doesn't keep an order.

newest-commit.explain: Newest first. The most recent work is always the most interesting, so it's on top.

what-is-a-branch.prompt: What does `git branch feature` actually create?

option.0: A movable label pointing at the current commit — nothing is copied.
option.1: A full copy of the entire project folder.
option.2: A new folder named `feature` inside your project.

what-is-a-branch.explain: A branch is just a pointer. That's why creating one is instant and free.

which-labels-move.prompt: You're on `feature` and commit. Which labels move?

option.2: No labels move; only the commit does.

which-labels-move.explain: A commit moves only the branch HEAD points to. That's how parallel work stays parallel.

why-no-new-commit.prompt: Your merge created NO new commit. Why?

option.1: `main` simply slid forward along `feature`'s existing commits — a fast-forward.
option.2: Git reuses the old commit and deletes `feature`.

why-no-new-commit.explain: When `main` hasn't diverged, there's nothing to combine — Git just moves the label. That's a fast-forward.

why-conflict.prompt: Why did Git pause the merge and ask for help?

option.0: Both sides changed the same line differently — only you can pick the final version.
option.1: Git crashed because two branches can't be merged.
option.2: The file was too large for an automatic merge.

why-conflict.explain: Git merges automatically when it can. When two edits touch the same spot, the decision needs a human.

undo-after-share.prompt: Your mistaken commit is already pushed and teammates have pulled it. Which undo is safer?

option.0: `git reset --hard` — it keeps the history cleaner.
option.1: `git revert` — it adds a correcting commit instead of rewriting shared history.
option.2: Delete the commit by hand from `.git`.

undo-after-share.explain: Never rewrite history others have built on. `revert` keeps the past intact and adds the correction on top.

stash-list-shows.prompt: After `git stash`, what does `git stash list` show?

option.0: Your shelved change — and the Working Tree stays clean until you pop it.
option.1: A list of all your commits, newest first.

stash-list-shows.explain: The stash is a shelf. `list` shows what's on it; the tree stays clean until `pop`.

option.0: Your `origin/main` pointer updated to match the remote — your files were not touched.
option.1: Your working files were overwritten with the remote versions.
option.2: Nothing — fetch is just a status command.

fetch-vs-pull.explain: Fetch updates knowledge. `origin/main` moved; integrating that into your work is a separate step (pull).

rebase-identities.prompt: Interactive rebase rewrites commits. What changes about them?

option.0: They get new identities (hashes) — the content is replayed on a new base.
option.1: Nothing — the same commits are just reordered in place.
option.2: They are deleted and never recoverable.

rebase-identities.explain: Replay means new commits with new hashes. The old ones still exist until garbage collection.

cherry-pick-vs-merge.prompt: Why would you cherry-pick instead of merge?

option.0: You want exactly one change from another branch, not its whole history.
option.1: Cherry-pick is faster than merge in every case.
option.2: Cherry-pick deletes the source branch for you.

cherry-pick-vs-merge.explain: Cherry-pick copies a single patch. Merge brings everything.

reset-lost-history.prompt: After `git reset --hard`, where does the 'lost' commit go?

option.1: It becomes unreachable but still exists — the reflog remembers it for a while.
option.2: It moves to the remote repository.

reset-lost-history.explain: Reset only moves the label. The commit stays until garbage collection; the reflog shows how to get back.

detached-head-save.prompt: You made commits while HEAD was detached. What keeps them safe?

option.0: Point a branch at them (e.g. `git switch -c rescue`) before leaving.
option.1: Nothing — detached commits are lost immediately.
option.2: Closing the terminal saves them automatically.

detached-head-save.explain: Commits need a named ref. A branch gives them one; otherwise they're only reachable via hash or reflog.

errors.notGit: Every command here starts with `git`. Try again with `git …`.
errors.generic: Git refused that command. Read the message above — it says why.
errors.typo: Almost — that's not a Git command. Check the spelling and try again.
errors.notARepository: Git isn't initialized here yet. There is nothing to inspect — create the repository first.
errors.nothingToCommit: Nothing was committed. Git only commits what is currently in the Staging Area.
errors.unsupportedSyntax: This simulator supports a fixed set of Git commands. Check the usage line above.
errors.unresolvedConflicts: Git can't continue while conflicts are open. Resolve them first.
errors.conflictNotEdited: Git won't stage a conflicted file you haven't resolved. Choose the final content first.
errors.operationInProgress: A merge or rebase is already in progress. Finish it before starting something new.
errors.unknownBranch: That branch doesn't exist. Check the graph or `git branch` to see the real names.
errors.unknownRevision: Git can't find that commit or branch. Check the spelling — hashes and names must match exactly.
errors.pathspecNotFound: Git can't find that file. Check the filename and try again.
errors.localChangesOverwritten: Git refused: this would destroy your unsaved changes. Commit or stash them first.
errors.noUpstream: This branch has no remote counterpart. Set an upstream or push explicitly.
errors.nonFastForward: The remote rejected the push: it has commits you don't have. Fetch and integrate first.
errors.noStash: The stash is empty. There is nothing to pop.
errors.branchExists: A branch with that name already exists. Pick a different name.
errors.deleteCurrentBranch: You can't delete the branch you're standing on. Switch away first.
errors.noCurrentBranch: Git needs to know which branch you mean.
errors.detachedMerge: You can't merge while HEAD is detached. Switch to a branch first.
errors.detachedRebase: You can't rebase while HEAD is detached. Switch to a branch first.
errors.tagExists: That tag already exists. Tags are one per name.
errors.remoteExists: That remote already exists. Check `git remote -v`.
errors.unknownRemote: That remote doesn't exist. Add it first, or check the spelling.
errors.emptyCherryPick: That commit has nothing to copy — it's already fully present here.
errors.operationBlocked: Git doesn't allow that operation right now.
errors.conflictCreated: That operation hit a conflict. Resolve it before continuing.
errors.interactiveRebaseUi: An interactive rebase needs a plan first — use the rebase editor above.
errors.invalidRebasePlan: That replay plan is not valid. Check the editor's choices.

b01.title: Meet Git
b01.scenario: Your project folder exists, with one file: `README.md`. Right now it is a normal folder — Git knows nothing about it yet.
b01.objective: Turn this normal folder into a Git repository.
b01.why: Every Git story starts here. Before Git can remember anything, it needs a place to write its history: the repository.
b01.mentalModel: `git init` creates a hidden folder called `.git` inside your project. That folder is Git's memory. Your files stay exactly where they are.
b01.commandIntro: You will run one command: `git init` — it means “initialize Git here”. The branch `main` is created, but it's empty: no commits yet.
b01.takeaway: Your folder is now a repository. `.git` exists, and `main` is waiting for its first commit.
hints: Git isn't watching your folder yet. There is exactly one command that makes Git “move in” and set up shop here.
The command means “initialize”. In Git, that word is `init`.
Type exactly: `git init`

b02.title: Your Three Git Zones
b02.scenario: Your repository has one file: `app.ts` — and it's still empty. Time for your first real change.
b02.objective: Change `app.ts`, stage it, and save your first commit.
b02.why: A commit is how Git saves your work — but it only saves what you explicitly select. Two steps make that visible: staging, then committing.
b02.mentalModel: Three zones: the Working Tree is your files right now. The Staging Area holds the versions you selected. The Repository keeps the saved history. Edit → stage → commit.
b02.commandIntro: After editing, you select the file with `git add app.ts` and save with `git commit -m "First snapshot"`. The `-m` part is the message describing your change.
b02.takeaway: You now know Git's golden rule: edit in the Working Tree, select with `add`, save with `commit`. Commits only contain what was staged.
hints: Right now your change lives only in the Working Tree — the leftmost zone. A commit never grabs files by itself: you must select them first.
Move the file into the Staging Area with `git add`, then turn the staged version into a commit with `git commit -m “…”`.
Run `git add app.ts`, then `git commit -m "First snapshot"`.

b03.title: See Your History
b03.scenario: Your project already has three commits — someone else made them yesterday. How do you find out what happened?
b03.objective: Inspect the history with `git log` and find the newest commit.
b03.why: History is Git's superpower. Reading it is how you answer: what changed, when, and why.
b03.mentalModel: Every commit has a unique ID — its hash — and points to its parent. Following parents backwards is reading history.
b03.commandIntro: `git log` lists commits, newest first. The flag `--oneline` squeezes each commit onto one line: short hash plus message. Try `git log --oneline`.
b03.takeaway: Commits form a chain through their parents. The short hashes are IDs you'll use later — to compare, undo, or recover.
hints: You want Git to tell its story. Which command asks Git to “show the history”?
The command is `git log`. A compact flag makes each commit fit on one line.
Run `git log --oneline`.

b04.title: Branches Without Fear
b04.scenario: Your teammate asks you to build a new feature — without touching the working main version. You need a parallel line of work.
b04.objective: Create a branch named `feature` and switch to it.
b04.why: Branches are why Git teams can work in parallel. Creating one costs nothing and copies nothing.
b04.mentalModel: A branch is just a movable label pointing at a commit. `HEAD` marks the branch you're working on. Creating a branch changes nothing in your files — switching moves HEAD.
b04.commandIntro: Two steps: `git branch feature` creates the label, `git switch feature` moves you onto it. Watch the graph: a second label appears, then HEAD jumps to it.
b04.takeaway: Branch = movable label. Switch = move HEAD. History is shared between branches — nothing gets copied.
hints: You need a second label in the graph first. What creates a new label at your current commit?
Create it with `git branch <name>`, then move onto it with `git switch <name>`.
Run `git branch feature`, then `git switch feature`.

b05.title: Build on a Branch
b05.scenario: You're on `feature` now. Ship two real changes — but `main` must stay exactly where it is.
b05.objective: Make two commits on `feature` without moving `main`.
b05.why: This is the everyday reality of branches: each branch advances only when you commit on it. `main` stays safe.
b05.mentalModel: When you commit, only the branch HEAD points to moves. `main`'s label doesn't budge — your two commits belong to `feature` alone.
b05.commandIntro: Edit the file in the editor (that changes the Working Tree, not Git). Then `git add .` — the dot means “everything changed” — and `git commit -m “…”`. Do it twice with different edits.
b05.takeaway: Commits only move the branch you're on. `main` is untouched — that's the safety branches give you.
hints: Where are you? `git status` shows the current branch. Commits land on the branch HEAD points to — make sure that's `feature`.
Each commit needs a staged change: edit the file, `git add .`, `git commit -m “...”`. Do it twice.
On `feature`: edit `app.ts`, `git add .`, `git commit -m "Feature work"` — then edit again, add, commit.

b06.title: Bring Work Together
b06.scenario: Your two feature commits are done and reviewed. Time to bring them into `main`.
b06.why: Merging is how separate lines of work become one. Understanding the fast-forward makes half of all merges feel obvious.
b06.mentalModel: You merge INTO the branch you're on. If `main` hasn't moved since you branched, Git simply slides `main` forward along the existing commits — a fast-forward. No new commit.
b06.commandIntro: First `git switch main` — Git merges into the branch you're on. Then `git merge feature`. Watch `main`'s label jump to the newest commit.
b06.takeaway: Fast-forward = no new commit, just a moved label. `main` now contains everything `feature` had.
hints: Which branch should receive the work? Git merges into the branch you're currently on.
Move to `main`, then bring `feature`'s history in.
Run `git switch main`, then `git merge feature`.

b07.title: Handle a Merge Conflict
b07.scenario: Two people changed the same line differently. Git merged everything it could — but this one spot needs your judgment.
b07.objective: Resolve the conflict in `app.ts` and finish the merge.
b07.why: Conflicts are not errors. They're Git asking you to be the human in the loop. Once you've seen one, they stop being scary.
b07.mentalModel: Git remembers the shared base and both versions: base = where you both started, ours = your branch, theirs = the incoming branch. You choose the final content.
b07.commandIntro: `git merge feature` will pause. The conflict panel shows base/ours/theirs. Choose the final content, then `git add app.ts` and `git commit -m "Resolve conflict"` to finish the merge.
b07.takeaway: A conflict means: Git needs a human decision. Resolve, stage, commit — the merge then completes with a commit that has two parents.
hints: Git paused the merge and is waiting. Look at the conflict panel: which two versions disagree?
Write the final content, then stage the file so Git knows it's resolved.
Resolve `app.ts`, run `git add app.ts`, then `git commit -m "Resolve conflict"`.

b08.title: Undo Without Guessing
b08.scenario: Your latest commit was a mistake. The question isn't “how do I undo?” — it's “which kind of undo?”
b08.objective: Try both undo strategies and see the difference: a reset and a revert.
b08.why: Panic-undoing is how people lose work. Knowing the difference between moving history and correcting it keeps you calm.
b08.mentalModel: `reset` moves the branch label backward — it rewrites local history. `revert` adds a NEW commit that undoes the old one — history keeps growing, which is safe to share.
b08.commandIntro: `HEAD~1` means “one commit before HEAD”. Try `git revert HEAD` first: watch a new correcting commit appear on top of history. Then `git reset --soft HEAD~1`: the label moves back and the reverted change lands in the Staging Area. Compare the graph each time.
b08.takeaway: Private history? Reset. Shared history? Revert. The graph shows you which one moved what.
hints: Two tools, one question: should a correcting commit be added, or should the label move backward?
`revert` grows history; `reset --soft` rewinds the label and keeps the changes staged. Try both and compare the graph.
Run `git revert HEAD`, then `git reset --soft HEAD~1` — and watch the X-Ray each time.

b09.title: Put Work Aside
b09.scenario: You're mid-change when an urgent bug fix comes in. You can't commit half-done work — but you need a clean tree right now.
b09.objective: Stash your changes, check that they're safely stored, then bring them back.
b09.why: Stash is Git's pause button for work-in-progress. You get a clean tree without losing (or committing) anything.
b09.mentalModel: A stash is a shelf: your changes are lifted off the Working Tree onto a stack. `pop` puts the top item back.
b09.commandIntro: `git stash` shelves your changes. `git stash list` shows the shelf. `git stash pop` puts them back into the Working Tree.
b09.takeaway: Stash = temporary shelf for work-in-progress. The tree became clean, then your work came back exactly as it was.
hints: You need a clean tree without a commit and without losing the changes. What Git feature lifts changes aside temporarily?
Put the changes on the stash stack, look at the stack, then restore the top entry.
Run `git stash`, then `git stash list`, then `git stash pop`.

b10.title: Understand Remotes
b10.scenario: Your code also lives on a server called `origin`, where teammates publish changes. Your local `main` and their `origin/main` are two different pointers.
b10.objective: Fetch from `origin`, then synchronize your branch as the state requires.
b10.why: Remotes are where collaboration happens. Local and remote-tracking branches are separate — fetch updates your knowledge, pull integrates, push publishes.
b10.mentalModel: `origin/main` is Git's local note about the remote — it only changes when you fetch. Fetch = update knowledge. Pull = fetch + merge. Push = publish your commits.
b10.commandIntro: Start with `git fetch origin` — watch `origin/main` move. Then decide: behind? `git pull`. Ahead? `git push -u origin main`.
b10.takeaway: Fetch ≠ pull ≠ push. Fetch updates knowledge, pull integrates, push publishes. Local and remote are always two separate things.
hints: Your local `main` and `origin/main` are two different pointers. Which command updates your knowledge of the remote?
Fetch first, then look at where `main` and `origin/main` point. If the remote is ahead, integrate it.
Run `git fetch origin`, then `git pull`.

a01.title: Interactive Rebase
a01.scenario: Your feature branch carries three messy “WIP” commits. Before sharing, turn them into one deliberate story.
a01.objective: Turn noisy feature history into deliberate history.
a01.why: Interactive rebase lets you edit how local commits are replayed.
a01.mentalModel: Replaying changes creates new commit identities.
a01.takeaway: The story reads cleanly now — and the replay produced new commit identities.
hints: Identify the local commits to rewrite.
Choose the correct rebase base.
Use pick/reword/squash/drop as the lesson requests.

a02.title: Cherry-Pick Surgery
a02.scenario: A hotfix landed on another branch. You want that one change — not the whole branch.
a02.objective: Copy one specific change onto your current branch.
a02.why: Cherry-pick is useful when you want one change, not the whole source branch.
a02.mentalModel: Git replays the selected commit change on a new parent, creating a new identity.
a02.takeaway: One patch, one new commit — the source branch was never touched.
hints: Find the source commit.
Replay that commit on the current branch.
Run `git cherry-pick <hash>`.

a03.title: Stash Like a Pro
a03.scenario: Several tasks are stacked on your desk. Each needs its own labeled shelf.
a03.why: A stash stack is useful only when you know what each entry represents.
a03.mentalModel: Each stash is temporary local state associated with a base and stack order.
a03.takeaway: Named entries, predictable order — context switching without losing the plot.
hints: Name the stash clearly.
Inspect the stack before applying.
Use `git stash -m "..."`, `git stash list`, then restore the intended entry.

a04.title: Reflog: Your Safety Net
a04.scenario: A hard reset just “deleted” two commits. They still exist — you just can't see them from a branch.
a04.objective: Recover commits that vanished from normal branch history.
a04.why: Many scary Git mistakes only move references. Reflog remembers previous HEAD positions.
a04.mentalModel: A commit can be unreachable from a branch without immediately ceasing to exist.
a04.takeaway: Reset moved the label — the work was never gone. The reflog knew where to find it.
hints: Inspect previous HEAD positions.
Find the lost tip in reflog.
Use `git reflog`, identify the old tip, then restore a branch/reference to it.

a05.title: Detached HEAD
a05.scenario: You jumped to an old commit to experiment. HEAD is now detached — and you just committed work here.
a05.objective: Experiment from an old commit and save the work safely.
a05.why: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch.
a05.mentalModel: Detached commits need a branch if you want an easy durable reference.
a05.takeaway: The experiment is safe on a named branch — HEAD is attached again.
hints: Notice whether HEAD is attached to a branch.
Create a branch pointing at the experimental work.
Use `git switch -c rescue` before leaving the detached work.

a06.title: Advanced Merge Reasoning
a06.scenario: Two branches changed adjacent parts of the same file. Git can merge most of it — one region needs you.
a06.objective: Resolve a non-trivial merge using base, ours and theirs.
a06.why: Three-way merge becomes predictable when you inspect the shared base.
a06.mentalModel: Git compares both sides against the merge base and combines compatible changes.
a06.takeaway: Compatible changes merged automatically; you decided the one real conflict.
hints: Identify the base and competing edits.
Resolve only the genuinely incompatible region.
Stage resolved files and complete the merge commit.

a07.title: Remote Divergence
a07.scenario: Your branch is ahead AND behind the remote at the same time. Both sides have work the other lacks.
a07.objective: Resolve a branch that is both ahead of and behind its remote.
a07.why: Fetch, pull and push make sense once local and remote-tracking refs are separate state.
a07.mentalModel: Divergence means each side has commits the other side lacks.
a07.takeaway: Fetch first, integrate, then push — divergence resolved in the right order.
hints: Fetch before deciding remote state.
Inspect ahead/behind.
Integrate remote work before pushing when the remote cannot fast-forward.

a08.title: Git Bisect
a08.scenario: A regression slipped in somewhere in fifty commits. Testing them one by one would take all day.
a08.objective: Find a regression by repeatedly halving the suspect history.
a08.why: Binary search can dramatically reduce the number of commits you must test.
a08.mentalModel: Mark known-good and known-bad points, then test useful midpoints.
a08.takeaway: Each step halves the suspects — fifty commits become a handful of tests.
hints: Start with good/bad boundaries.
Classify the midpoint.
Repeat until the first bad commit remains.

a09.title: Submodules vs Subtrees
a09.scenario: You need a shared library inside two projects. Two very different Git strategies promise this.
a09.objective: Understand two repository-composition approaches without pretending they are the same.
a09.why: Both connect projects, but ownership/update mechanics differ.
a09.mentalModel: A submodule records a pointer to another repo state; a subtree brings another project content into your history.
a09.takeaway: Pointer vs. integrated content — the choice shapes how updates flow.
hints: Focus on where nested history lives.
Compare pointer-based composition with integrated content.
Classify each visual scenario as submodule or subtree.

a10.title: Git Internals
a10.scenario: Everything in Git is content-addressed objects. Time to see the chain that holds it all together.
a10.objective: Trace a file from blob to tree to commit to branch ref.
a10.why: Git becomes less magical once you see that commits point to trees and refs point to commits.
a10.mentalModel: Content objects are immutable; movable refs name points in that object graph.
a10.takeaway: blob → tree → commit → ref: the whole architecture in one chain.
hints: Start from file content.
Follow blob → tree → commit.
Then identify the ref that gives the commit a human-friendly name.
